newsitem.title: JAPAN: Follower of Japan cult guru refuses to testify.
newsitem.headline: Follower of Japan cult guru refuses to testify.

text.p: A top follower of the Japanese doomsday cult guru on trial for last year's Tokyo subway nerve-gas attack refused to testify in court on Thursday, saying he was given no time to talk to his chief attorney.

But Seiichi Endo, 36, one of two cult biochemists accused of mass-producing the deadly nerve gas sarin used in the March 20, 1995, attack, said he would testify in a few months once he sees his lawyer and discusses ways to avoid self-incrimination.
"I refuse to testify now," Endo told the Tokyo District Court, as his hands shook slightly with tension. "I will be able to testify and tell the truth after I discuss matters with my chief lawyer."
Endo is the third top disciple of guru Shoko Asahara, 41, to appear in the guru's trial. Endo himself is on separate trial for murder linked to the subway attack.
Endo's lawyer has been sick and is in hospital, he added.
Two other followers, cult doctor Ikuo Hayashi and gas-attack team leader Yoshihiro Inoue, testified against their former guru in separate court appearances last month.
Asahara has been charged with murder and attempted murder in the subway gas attack, which killed 11 people and harmed more than 5,500. He has not entered a plea.
Asahara is on trial on 16 other charges, ranging from illegal drugs and weapons production to murder, kidnap and attempted murder. The maximum penalty for a single murder charge is death by hanging.

In Thursday's session, the 10th in Asahara's trial which opened last April, the defence cross-examined a subway platform official, and seven police officers who conducted the initial investigation after the attack.

Still sporting his trademark long hair and beard, Asahara sat impassively throughout as police officers revealed shocking subway platform scenes after the sarin was released, of dozens of passengers collapsing and some coming down with severe seizures. Asahara was not asked to speak in Thursday's session.
After a series of meticulous questions on the exact location of the plastic bags containing the sarin liquid, the defence launched another round of bitter criticism against the prosecution.
"The prosecutor's opening statement is too nebulous," said Osamu Watanabe, who heads Asahara's team of nine state-appointed lawyers. "It does not clearly explain the details of the murder charge."
Watanabe said the prosecution carried out a "sneak attack" by asking disciple Inoue to testify, without giving the defence a chance to examine his affidavits beforehand.
